Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: The introduction frames guitar as a physical and expressive activity: the more consistently and intelligently the player practices, the more freedom they gain. It also presents exercises as movable forms that can travel around the neck.
Hearth Application: Use this as a bridge between Foundation and Doing: guitar learning is not just information, it is trained movement. The guide can frame practice as earning freedom in the hands.
Notes: Printed page 1 starts on PDF page 17.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: The book emphasizes movable scale, arpeggio, and chord patterns: once the fingering is learned, the same form can shift to new keys by moving the starting point.
Hearth Application: This supports the Hearth idea of shapes as portable spells: one pattern, many locations. It should inform early explanations of fretboard shapes, transposition, and root-note awareness.
Notes: Good bridge to QJam scale-pattern progression.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Concept: Three exercise families: scales arpeggios chords
Source Summary: The book organizes the bulk of practice into scales, arpeggios, and chords, with sequences and progressions as the next layer of difficulty.
Hearth Application: Use this as a simple Doing taxonomy: single-note maps, broken-chord maps, and chord movement. This can help make the practice surface feel less random.
Notes: Useful for database categories and drill grouping.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: Chapter 1 reviews holding the guitar, sitting/standing position, and how to read tab, chord diagrams, neck diagrams, and rhythm slashes before beginning exercises.
Hearth Application: Foundation should not assume the learner knows the symbols. Before drills, the app should teach the physical setup and the map symbols that make drills readable.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: The chapter emphasizes choosing a guitar position that is comfortable and consistent rather than fashionable.
Hearth Application: Hearth voice: the guitar should become a repeatable home position, not a costume. This supports posture guidance: supported, consistent, not clamped.
Notes: Pairs well with Jamie Andreas once OCRed.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: The book explains chord diagrams and neck diagrams as visual maps for finger placement, finger numbers, roots, tonics, and movable forms.
Hearth Application: Use this to build visual literacy in Foundation/Study: diagrams are not decorations, they are maps. The learner should know what dots, numbers, roots, and tonics mean.
Notes: Good source for a Study node micro-lesson on diagrams.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Concept: Warming up the body and mind
Source Summary: Chapter 2 frames warm-up as preparation for better playing, not optional fluff. It includes loosening fingers, relaxing the body, maintaining focus, and using simple single-note and chord exercises.
Hearth Application: This directly supports the Hearth ritual of entering practice: body scan, loosen hands, focus attention, then play. Warm-up becomes a threshold, not a chore.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: The text asks the player to relax the body after practice and notice stored tension, especially in shoulders and larger muscle groups.
Hearth Application: Use this in the Practice node reflection: after playing, check what the body kept holding. This connects technique to nervous-system awareness.
Notes: Strong link to whole-person / neurological reflection.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: The chapter treats focus as part of practice preparation rather than a vague personality trait.
Hearth Application: Practice sessions should include an intention step: what are you listening for, what are you correcting, what will count as clean enough?
Notes: Supports intention -> timer -> practice -> reflect flow.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Concept: Pattern exercises across and diagonally along the neck
Source Summary: Warm-up patterns are described as repeated finger movements across the neck and diagonally up the neck, with the musical meaning less important than clean physical patterning.
Hearth Application: Use as early Doing drills: pattern first, speed later. The guide should explain that some exercises are not songs; they are coordination rituals for the hands.
Notes: Useful for first chromatic/warm-up drill design.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Concept: Major scales as usable playing material
Source Summary: Chapter 3 begins the scale section by putting major scale patterns to use, including multiple patterns and application to recognizable pieces.
Hearth Application: When scales arrive, they should not feel like abstract homework. The app should connect each pattern to sound, song fragments, and musical use.
Notes: Chapter-level note from TOC and chapter placement; needs deeper pass later.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: Chapter 4 develops major scale sequences, turning a plain scale pattern into repeated ordered movements that build fluency and variation.
Hearth Application: This supports the Doing node after basic scale shapes: sequence practice teaches the hands to speak in phrases instead of alphabet recitation.
Notes: Needs concept-level extraction in a later pass.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: Chapters 5 and 6 cover natural, harmonic, and melodic minor scales and minor scale sequences.
Hearth Application: Use as later Knowing/Doing material: minor is not one mood, but a family of related sounds. This should come after basic pentatonic and major-scale grounding.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: Part III introduces major, minor, and seventh-chord arpeggios, including patterns and sequences. The structure links broken chords to harmonic understanding.
Hearth Application: Arpeggios should be taught as chords unfolded into motion. This bridges Knowing and Doing: harmony becomes something the hand can travel through.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: Part IV moves into chord exercises, chord progressions, and moving along the neck, including climbing/descending strings and diagonal movement.
Hearth Application: Use this to frame chord work as movement, not static grips. A chord is not 'known' until it can move into another chord or another location.

Author: Mark Phillips & Jon Chappell
Source Summary: Chapter 15 gives practice advice: define practice place and time, set objectives, keep accessories ready, focus mentally, warm up, start slow, isolate difficult passages, vary guitars, and seek community.
Hearth Application: This should feed the Practice node's session design. The app can ask: what is today's objective, what is the hard passage, what tempo is honest, and what is the next small step?
Notes: Excellent source for Practice node UX.
